questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two different routes give the same joint probability
questions.stem: A manufacturer has two plants. Plant A makes 70 percent of output with a 2 percent defect rate and plant B makes 30 percent with a 6 percent rate. Explain, using two different routes, the probability that a randomly chosen item is both from plant B and defective, and give the value.

answer.exemplar: Route one multiplies the chance an item comes from plant B, which is 0.30, by the chance such an item is defective, which is 0.06, giving 0.018. Route two counts outcomes instead: in 1000 items, 300 come from plant B and 6 percent of 300 is 18, so 18 of 1000 items are both, which is 0.018 again. The two agree because the second rate is already conditional on the plant.

questions.explanation: Multiplying 0.30 by 0.06 gives 0.018 because the 0.06 is already conditional on plant B. Counting 18 out of 1000 items in that plant reproduces the figure, confirming both routes agree.
questions.hint: One route multiplies, the other counts.

questions.stem: A graph shows two lines that never meet and a second graph shows two lines lying exactly on top of each other. Explain how each picture classifies the system formed by those lines, and why the pictures differ.

answer.exemplar: The two never-meeting lines are distinct parallel lines: they share a slope but not a y-intercept, so the system they represent has no solution. The two coinciding lines are the same line written twice, so every point on it satisfies both equations and the system has infinitely many solutions. The deciding factor is whether the intercepts match as well as the slopes.

questions.explanation: Distinct parallel lines give a system with no solution, while identical coinciding lines give infinitely many solutions. Matching slopes alone is not enough; the y-intercepts must also match for the lines to be the same.
questions.hint: Compare both slope and intercept.

questions.learningObjective: Reduce a system to one equation in x using substitution
questions.stem: A planner must solve 2x + 3y = 21 and x - y = 3. Explain, step by step, how substitution turns this into a single equation in x, and state the value of x you obtain.

answer.exemplar: First isolate y in the second equation: x - y = 3 gives y = x - 3. Substitute that expression for y in the first equation to get 2x + 3(x - 3) = 21, which expands to 2x + 3x - 9 = 21 and then 5x = 30. Dividing by 5 gives x = 6, and the matching value of y is 3, which checks back in both equations.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a conditional share differs from a base rate
questions.stem: A bank approves 90 percent of applications from salaried applicants and 60 percent of applications from self-employed applicants, and 70 percent of its applicants are salaried. Explain, using two routes, the probability that a randomly chosen approved applicant is salaried.

answer.exemplar: Route one works with probabilities: the share of salaried applicants who are approved is 0.7 times 0.9, which is 0.63, and the share of all applicants approved is 0.7 times 0.9 plus 0.3 times 0.6, which is 0.81, so the conditional share is 0.63 divided by 0.81, about 0.778. questions.explanation: Multiplying 0.7 by 0.9 and dividing by the overall approval rate 0.81 gives about 0.778. Counting 63 approved salaried applicants out of 81 approved total confirms the same figure.

answer.exemplar: Start with the equation that already has y alone on one side: 2x - y = 8 gives y = 2x - 8.
